chunks: Sources of reflection on a PCB and fixes. The question: Describe some sources of reflection on a PCB (any any interfaces). How can these reflections be minimized?
A reflection happens wherever a wave hits a change in impedance. Part of the signal keeps going and part bounces back.
On a board, impedance changes at the driver and receiver ends, at stubs and branches, vias, pads, connectors, width changes and gaps in the plane.
You fix them by removing the change, making it small, or adding a termination that absorbs the bounce.
Imagine a rope with a heavy knot in the middle. Send a pulse down the rope and part of it reflects back at the knot. A smooth, uniform rope has no reflection.
Now tie the far end to a wall, and the pulse bounces fully back. The knot is a bad via or a stub. The wall is an unterminated receiver. A damper at the end soaks up the bounce.
An illustrative TDR profile. A pad is a dip (shunt C), a via is a peak then a dip (series L then C), a neck-down is a peak, and the termination mismatch shows as a step.
Because TDR plots impedance against time, you can read each discontinuity's position (1 nanoseconds of round trip about 85 mm of line) and sign.
Profile values are schematic, not measured.
Reflection coefficient ( ): (Z 2 minus Z 1) over (Z 2 plus Z 1) , the fraction that bounces back ("Reflections and why they matter").
Stub: a dead-end branch off a line ("What causes reflections"). Termination: a resistor that matches the line so the wave is absorbed ("Termination networks").
Ringing: oscillation from repeated reflections between mismatched ends. TDR: a measurement that shows impedance along a line using a fast step.
A wave on a 50 ohms line hits an open receiver. With Z L to infinity , equals plus 1 , so the voltage at the end doubles. Now a T-junction splits the line into two 50 ohms lines.
The wave sees 50 50 equals 25 ohms, so equals (25 minus 50) over (25 plus 50) equals -1 over 3 . A third of the wave bounces back. That is the whole idea.
"A reflection occurs wherever the impedance seen by the wave changes: equals (Z L-Z 0) over (Z L plus Z 0) .
On a board that means the driver and receiver ends, stubs and T-junctions, vias, pads, connectors, width and layer changes, and gaps in the reference plane.

I minimise them by avoiding the discontinuity, making the unavoidable ones small compared with the edge, and terminating the line so any remaining reflection is absorbed, then verifying with simulation or TDR."
